Asymmetric and Heavy-Tailed GARCH: EGARCH, GJR, and Student-t
Fixing the structural defects of GARCH(1,1) for honest VaR and Expected Shortfall in crypto.

The Leverage Effect, and Why Crypto Is Messier
e The Equity Baseline (Black, 1976): Bad news lowers equity value, raises leverage, and spikes future volatility more than equally-sized good news.
e The Crypto Reality: No corporate balance-sheet leverage. Asymmetry persists via forced liquidations of over-collateralized loans and perp longs.

The Messy Caveat: Violent up-moves (squeezes, ETF gaps) also spike volatility. Asymmetry must be treated as an empirical question, not a strict law.

Summary

References

Plain GARCH(1,1) costs money via optimistic VaR; it ignores
asymmetry and Gaussian tails.

GJR-GARCH captures asymmetry via threshold (\gamma > @ = downside
asymmetry); requires positivity constraints.

EGARCH captures asymmetry via log-variance (\gamma < @ = downside
asymmetry); avoids positivity constraints. Verified via News
Impact Curve.

Student-t and Skew-t expose the true depth of crypto’s left tail,
inflating VaR and Expected Shortfall to honest levels.

Backtest out-of-sample with Kupiec and Christoffersen. Reject
models that cluster violations. Add complexity only when BIC and
walk-forward VaR demand it.
